blocks.text: A microcontroller pin can source about 20 mA at 3.3 V, yet it can start a 12 V, 5 A pump motor. The trick is to let the pin control a transistor that does the heavy lifting: a switch with a tiny control current in and a large load current through. Choosing the right component values decides whether the transistor runs cool or cooks itself.

blocks.markdown: A **transistor switch** operates in only two states: fully **off** (almost no current, large voltage across it) and fully **on** (large current, small voltage across it). Power dissipated in the transistor is $v\times i$, so in either state it is small; the danger is the transitional or half-on region where both are significant. Two families dominate: the **bipolar junction transistor (BJT)**, controlled by base current, and the **MOSFET**, controlled by gate voltage.

blocks.title: BJT saturation
blocks.text: An NPN BJT used as a switch has the load in the collector and the emitter at ground. To turn it **fully on (saturation)** the base current must be more than the collector current requires in the active region: $I_B>I_C/\beta_{min}$, where $\beta_{min}$ is the minimum guaranteed current gain on the datasheet. In saturation the collector-emitter voltage falls to $V_{CE(sat)}\approx0.1$ to 0.3 V (typical) and the base-emitter voltage is $V_{BE}\approx0.7$ V.

blocks.title: Choosing the base resistor
blocks.prompt: A relay coil draws $I_C=80$ mA from a 12 V supply. An NPN BJT has $\beta_{min}=100$. A 5 V logic output drives its base through a resistor. Choose the resistor with an overdrive factor of 5.

steps.text: Base current to just saturate, then with overdrive.
Base resistor from KVL around the input loop, with $V_{BE}=0.7$ V.
Choose the nearest standard value below (so the base current is at least that wanted) and check.

blocks.answer: Use 1.0 kohm: the base current is 4.3 mA, more than five times the 0.8 mA minimum, so the transistor saturates. A flyback diode across the relay coil is also needed.

blocks.markdown: **MOSFET as a low-side switch.** An N-channel enhancement MOSFET has a **gate**, **drain** and **source**. In a **low-side** configuration the load sits between the positive supply and the drain, and the source is grounded. When the gate-source voltage $V_{GS}$ exceeds the threshold $V_{th}$ (and, for a switch, is well above it, e.g. 4.5 V for a 'logic-level' device) a conducting channel forms and the drain-source path acts as a small resistor $R_{DS(on)}$ (milliohms to tens of milliohms). The gate draws essentially no steady current, so the microcontroller needs only to charge a small capacitance. Below $V_{th}$ the channel is off.

blocks.caption: On-state dissipation in a MOSFET switch

blocks.title: Conduction loss comparison
blocks.prompt: A 12 V DC motor draws 5.0 A. Compare the on-state power in a logic-level MOSFET with $R_{DS(on)}=40$ mohm and in a BJT with $V_{CE(sat)}=0.30$ V.
blocks.answer: The MOSFET dissipates 1.0 W against 1.5 W for the BJT, and its loss scales with current squared, so at lower current it wins even more; the BJT also needs a large base current (about 0.5 A at a forced gain of 10).

rows: Motors, solenoids, PWM at higher currents
blocks.caption: BJT versus MOSFET as low-side switches

items: Always add a flyback diode across an inductive load (relay, motor, solenoid).
A BJT needs a series base resistor; a MOSFET benefits from a gate series resistor (tens of ohms) and a pull-down resistor (about 10 k$\Omega$) to keep it off when the pin floats.
Check that $V_{GS}$ from the logic output reaches the voltage at which $R_{DS(on)}$ is specified.
Check power: $P=I^2R_{DS(on)}$ and compare with the device's rating and heatsinking.

blocks.title: Underdriving a BJT or MOSFET
blocks.text: A BJT given too little base current, or a MOSFET with too little gate voltage, sits in its active (linear) region with both a large voltage and a large current, so it dissipates far more power and can overheat. A switch must be driven hard on or fully off.

points: Saturate a BJT with $I_B\ge k\,I_C/\beta_{min}$ and set $R_B=(V_{in}-0.7)/I_B$.
An N-MOSFET low-side switch conducts when $V_{GS}$ is well above $V_{th}$ and behaves as a small resistor $R_{DS(on)}$.
On-state power is $I_CV_{CE(sat)}$ for a BJT and $I_D^2R_{DS(on)}$ for a MOSFET.

questions.stem: A BJT switches a 50 mA relay coil. Its minimum current gain is 100. What is the smallest base current that just supports saturation?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is a factor of 10 too large.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this equates base and collector currents.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a factor of 10 too small.

questions.explanation: The minimum base current is $I_C/\beta_{min}=50/100=0.5$ mA. In practice a margin of 3 to 5 times is used to make sure saturation is reached.

questions.stem: How is an N-channel MOSFET connected as a low-side switch for a load?

options.text: Load between the supply and drain, source to ground, gate driven by the logic signal
Load between the source and ground, drain to the supply
Gate connected to the supply through the load

questions.correctOptionText: Load between the supply and drain, source to ground, gate driven by the logic signal

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the load is on the high side of the MOSFET and the MOSFET is between load and ground.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is a source-follower (high-side) arrangement and needs a higher gate voltage.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the gate is the control terminal and carries no load current.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the gate must be driven by the control signal.

questions.explanation: A low-side switch interrupts the return path: the load connects to the positive supply, and the MOSFET connects the load's other end (drain) to ground via the source.

questions.stem: A MOSFET with $R_{DS(on)}=0.05$ ohm conducts 3.0 A continuously. What is the power dissipated in it?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is I x R = 0.15 V, the drop in volts, not power.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is I^2 with no R.

questions.explanation: $P=I^2R_{DS(on)}=3.0^2\times0.05=0.45$ W. Equivalently, the drop is $V=IR=0.15$ V and $P=VI=0.15\times3.0=0.45$ W.

questions.stem: A 3.3 V logic pin drives an NPN BJT through $R_B$ to switch a 200 mA load. $\beta_{min}=50$, $V_{BE}=0.7$ V and the overdrive factor is 3. Which base resistor is suitable?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this omits the overdrive factor (I_B = 4 mA).
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this forgets to subtract V_BE (3.3/12 mA).
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this uses I_B = 1 mA, ignoring the required current.

questions.explanation: Base current is $3\times0.200/50=12$ mA. The resistor drops $3.3-0.7=2.6$ V, so $R_B=2.6/0.012=217$ ohm. A 220 ohm standard value gives 11.8 mA.

questions.stem: Why is a pull-down resistor (about 10 k$\Omega$) often fitted between the gate and ground of a low-side MOSFET driven by a microcontroller?

options.text: To hold the gate low, keeping the MOSFET off while the pin is floating (e.g. at reset)
To reduce the drain current in the on state
To protect the load from reverse voltage

questions.correctOptionText: To hold the gate low, keeping the MOSFET off while the pin is floating (e.g. at reset)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a floating gate may drift above threshold and switch the load on unintentionally.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a pull-down cannot raise the voltage.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: drain current is set by the load and R_DS(on).
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: reverse voltage protection is by a diode.

questions.explanation: The gate is a high-impedance node. If the controller pin is floating, charge or noise can turn the MOSFET on. A pull-down resistor defines the gate at 0 V by default.

questions.stem: An NPN BJT must switch 120 mA with $\beta_{min}=80$. A 5.0 V output drives the base resistor, $V_{BE}=0.7$ V, and the overdrive factor is 5. What base resistance is needed, in ohms?
questions.explanation: $I_B=5\times0.120/80=7.5$ mA. $R_B=(5.0-0.7)/0.0075=573$ ohm. A standard 560 ohm resistor gives 7.7 mA.

questions.stem: A BJT switch carries 0.50 A with $V_{CE(sat)}=0.25$ V. What power does it dissipate in the on state, in milliwatts? (Ignore base drive power.)
A 24 V supply drives a 6.0 ohm resistive load through a MOSFET low-side switch whose $R_{DS(on)}$ is 0.15 ohm. What power (in watts) is dissipated in the MOSFET?
questions.explanation: The on-state circuit has total resistance $6.0+0.15=6.15$ ohm, so $I=24/6.15=3.902$ A. Then $P=I^2R_{DS(on)}=3.902^2\times0.15=2.28$ W. Note the current is not $24/6=4$ A because the switch resistance is in series.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between the active and saturation regions of a BJT switch, and why the base current is chosen larger than $I_C/\beta_{min}$. What happens if the base resistor is too large?
markingGuide: Active region: I_C = beta I_B and V_CE is large; saturation: V_CE small (about 0.1 to 0.3 V) and I_C limited by the load
Switch must be in saturation to dissipate little power
Beta varies with temperature and between devices, so a margin (overdrive 3 to 5) ensures saturation
If R_B too large, I_B too small: transistor stays in active region with large V_CE
Large V_CE x I_C gives high dissipation, overheating, and the load receives less voltage
questions.explanation: In the active region the collector current is $\beta I_B$ and the collector-emitter voltage is large, while in saturation $V_{CE}$ is only about 0.2 V and the load sets the current. Because $\beta$ varies from device to device and with temperature, the base current is made several times $I_C/\beta_{min}$ to ensure saturation. If $R_B$ is too large the transistor falls into the active region with both high $V_{CE}$ and high $I_C$, dissipating a lot of heat and starving the load.

questions.stem: A 12 V solenoid taking 2.0 A is switched by a logic-level N-MOSFET with $R_{DS(on)}=40$ mohm at 4.5 V gate drive. Describe the low-side circuit connections, explain how the MOSFET turns the solenoid on and off, calculate the on-state MOSFET power, and state any protection component needed.
markingGuide: Solenoid between +12 V and drain; source to ground; gate driven by logic output (with series resistor and pull-down)
V_GS above threshold forms a channel, resistance R_DS(on): current flows; V_GS = 0 turns it off
Voltage drop across the MOSFET on-state = 0.08 V so the solenoid receives almost the full 12 V
Flyback diode across the solenoid (cathode to +12 V) to clamp the inductive turn-off spike
questions.explanation: The solenoid connects between +12 V and the drain, and the source is grounded; the logic signal drives the gate (with a small series resistor and a pull-down). When $V_{GS}$ exceeds the threshold a channel forms with resistance $R_{DS(on)}=40$ mohm, so the on-state loss is $2.0^2\times0.040=0.16$ W and the voltage drop only 0.08 V. At turn-off the solenoid's inductance would create a voltage spike, so a flyback diode with its cathode at +12 V is placed across it.
